introduction-why-most-strategy-is-blind.core: Most strategy documents are lists of actions without a map of the landscape. Wardley Mapping visualises the components that serve a user need and how evolved each is, giving situational awareness before you choose moves.

first_principles.problem: A general handed a list ('we have tanks, we should attack') without a map of the terrain makes blind decisions.
truths: Context determines which moves make sense.

analogy.title: A battle map vs. a list of assets
analogy.story: The map shows terrain, positions and movement; the list doesn't.
analogy.breaks: Maps are models: useful but imperfect, and dependent on judgement.

example.title: A list vs a map
flow: List: build own auth, own DB, own ML platform
Map: auth and DB are commodities → buy

check.q: What does a Wardley Map add that a strategy list lacks?
check.a: Situational awareness: how components serve a user need and how evolved each is.

the-axes-value-chain-and-evolution.core: The Y-axis is the value chain: the user need at the top, then components ordered by visibility to the user (visible at the top, hidden infrastructure at the bottom). The X-axis is evolution: Genesis → Custom-built → Product/rental → Commodity/utility.

first_principles.problem: Without precise axes, maps become arbitrary diagrams that can't guide decisions.
truths: Components depend on others below them.
Everything evolves toward commodity over time.

analogy.title: Electricity's evolution
analogy.story: It went from lab curiosity (genesis) to custom generators, then products, then a utility you plug into.
analogy.breaks: Placement is a judgement call, so discuss it in teams to calibrate.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A clear picture of what's novel and what's utility.

check.q: What are the four evolution stages on a Wardley Map?

the-golden-rule-match-your-investment-to.core: Treat each component according to its stage. Genesis needs exploration and agile experimentation, custom-built needs skilled teams building differentiation, product means buying or standardising, and commodity means renting a utility. Building commodities in-house wastes money; outsourcing genesis loses your edge.

first_principles.problem: Companies build their own databases and authentication (commodities) while outsourcing their core differentiator.
truths: Differentiation lives in the less-evolved components.

analogy.title: Cooking at a restaurant
analogy.story: You invent your signature dish in-house but buy salt and electricity.
analogy.breaks: Strategic reasons (data sovereignty, cost at huge scale) sometimes justify building commodities.

check.q: Why is building a commodity component in-house usually a mistake?
check.a: Commodities are cheaper and more reliable to rent, so in-house effort wastes resources better spent on differentiation.

reading-and-drawing-a-wardley-map-step-b.core: To draw a map: (1) identify the user and their need, (2) list the components that fulfil it, (3) arrange them by dependency and visibility, (4) place each on the evolution axis, (5) add movement (arrows for expected evolution), and (6) look for strategic opportunities and risks.

first_principles.problem: Teams know the theory but don't know how to start drawing a useful map.

analogy.title: Drawing a subway map
analogy.story: Start from destinations people want, add the lines connecting them, and mark lines under construction.
analogy.breaks: First maps are rough. Iterate with colleagues.

example.title: Mapping an internal developer platform
flow: User: product engineers → need: ship features safely
Components: CI, deploy, observability, K8s, compute
Placement: K8s/compute commodity; golden paths custom
Arrow: deploy tooling moving to product

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Invest in golden paths and adopt managed K8s.

example.outcome: maps you can draw and use.

check.q: What's the first step in drawing a Wardley Map?
check.a: Identify the user and their need, which anchors the top of the map.

wardley-mapping-in-practice-common-patte.core: In practice, maps reveal patterns: inertia (resisting the commoditisation of something you built), the build-vs-buy wrongly calibrated, opportunities to commoditise a competitor's differentiator, and climatic patterns like evolution driven by competition. They fail when made alone, treated as precise, or never acted on.

first_principles.problem: Teams draw beautiful maps that no one uses, or argue endlessly about exact placements.
truths: Maps are for communication and decisions.
derivation: Look for **inertia**: legacy custom builds of now-commodity components.
Spot **opportunities**: commoditise a layer, or exploit an ecosystem.
Use maps in **group discussions**, not as solo artefacts.
**Act and revisit**: maps change as the landscape evolves.

analogy.title: A weather map in a planning meeting
analogy.story: Its value comes from deciding whether to launch the boat, not from admiring the isobars.
analogy.breaks: Over-emphasising mapping can delay action, so time-box it.

example.title: Inertia spotted
flow: Group notes managed observability is now commodity
Decision: migrate; authors lead new ML work

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Effort is freed for higher-value work.

check.a: Resistance to changing how a component is provided (for example, keeping a custom build) even after it has become a commodity.
